lessons.title: Folders, paths and your home
lessons.summary: How files are organized on Geiss-01, and the two commands that tell you where you are and what is around you.

blocks.text:
Everything on Geiss-01 lives in one big tree of folders (Linux calls them directories). The top of the tree is `/`, called the root. Every other folder hangs below it: `/home`, `/scratch`, `/opt`, and so on.

You have your own folder at `/home/student`. It's called your home folder, and the shortcut `~` (tilde) always means it. When you log in, you start there.

example.out:
/
├── home/
│   └── student/          ← your home folder, also called ~
│       ├── binder_design/
│       │   ├── inputs/
│       │   └── runs/
│       └── notes.txt
├── scratch/              ← big, fast, temporary space
└── opt/                  ← installed software
example.note: A path names a spot in this tree by listing the folders on the way, separated by `/`. `/home/student/binder_design/inputs` means: start at the root, go into home, then student, then binder_design, then inputs.

blocks.text: At any moment your terminal is "in" one folder, called the working directory. Commands look for files there unless you say otherwise. The prompt shows it: `student@geiss-01:~$` means you are in `~`.

command.name: pwd
command.what: Prints the full path of the folder you are in. Use it whenever you're not sure where you are.

try.text: Type `pwd` and press Enter to see where you start.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

try.hint: Type the three letters pwd, then press Enter.

command.name: ls
command.what: Lists what is in a folder. With no folder named, it lists the folder you are in. Folders are shown in blue here.

try.text: List what's in your home folder with `ls`.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

blocks.text: You can also list a folder without going into it: `ls binder_design` shows what is inside binder_design, and you stay where you are.

try.text: List the inside of `binder_design` without moving.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

try.hint: Put the folder name after ls, with a space: ls binder_design

quiz.q: You type `pwd` and see `/home/student/binder_design/inputs`. Which folder are you in?
quiz.why: pwd prints the whole path from the root, and the last name is the folder you are in. The names before it are the folders that contain it.

lessons.title: Moving around with cd
lessons.summary: Step into folders, climb back out, and jump home.

command.name: cd
command.what: Moves you into another folder. It prints nothing when it works; the prompt changes to show where you are now.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

blocks.text: Three special names work with `cd` and almost every other command:

flags: The folder one level up, the one that contains this one
The folder you are in right now

example.note: From `~/binder_design/inputs`, `cd ..` takes you up to `~/binder_design`. Run it again and you're back in `~`.

blocks.tip: Plain `cd` with nothing after it also takes you home. It's the quickest way back when you're lost.

try.text: You're deep inside a run folder. Climb up one level with `..`.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

try.hint: cd ..  (cd, a space, then two dots)

try.text: Now jump straight home in one move.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

quiz.q: You are in `~/binder_design/runs`. Where does `cd ..` take you?
quiz.why: .. is the parent: the folder that holds the one you're in. runs sits inside binder_design.

lessons.title: Hidden files and ls options
lessons.summary: What the letters after a dash do, and the files ls doesn't show you.

blocks.text: Most commands take options (also called flags) that change what they do. An option starts with a dash: `ls -a`. Single letters can be combined: `ls -la` is the same as `ls -l -a`.
Files and folders whose names start with a dot, like `.bashrc`, are hidden: plain `ls` skips them. Programs keep their settings in hidden files so they don't clutter your listing.

flags: Show hidden files too, including . and ..
One line per file: permissions, owner, size, date
With -l, sizes like 4.0K and 12M instead of bytes
Also list every folder inside, all the way down

try.text: Show everything in your home folder, hidden files included.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

example.out:
drwxr-xr-x 4 student student 4.0K Oct 24 09:12 binder_design
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student   27 Oct 24 09:10 notes.txt
example.note: The first letter is `d` for a folder and `-` for a file. Then come permissions, owner, size, the date it last changed, and the name.

try.text: Get the long listing with readable sizes.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

quiz.q: Which command lists hidden files, one per line, with sizes like 12M?
quiz.why: -a adds hidden files, -l gives one line per file with details, and -h makes the sizes readable.

lessons.title: Relative and absolute paths
lessons.summary: Go several folders at once, and name any folder from anywhere.

blocks.text: You don't have to `cd` one folder at a time. Join the names with `/` and go in one move: `cd binder_design/runs/run1`.

A path that starts from where you are is a relative path. A path that starts with `/` is an absolute path: it starts at the root, so it works the same from any folder. `~/...` counts as absolute too, because `~` always means `/home/student`.

flags: From the folder you're in, go into runs, then run1
From the root, wherever you are
From your home folder, wherever you are
Up one level, then into run2

try.text: From home, go straight to `binder_design/runs/run1/outputs` in one command.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

try.text: You're in run1. Move sideways into run2 using `..`.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

try.hint: Go up to runs, then down into run2: cd ../run2

blocks.tip: Press Tab while typing a name and the terminal finishes it for you. If nothing happens, press Tab twice to see the choices. It saves typing and catches typos.

quiz.q: You're in `/scratch/student`. Which command takes you to `/home/student/binder_design`?
quiz.why: ~/binder_design works from anywhere because it starts at your home folder. The others look for binder_design next to where you are, or at the root.

lessons.title: Capitals, spaces and going back
lessons.summary: Small details that trip people up: case, spaces in names, and cd -.

blocks.text: Linux treats upper and lower case as different letters. `Projects` and `projects` are two different names, and `cd projects` fails if the folder is really called `Projects`.

A space separates the parts of a command, so a name with a space in it confuses `cd`: `cd my runs` looks like two names. Put the name in quotes, `cd "my runs"`, or put a backslash before the space, `cd my\ runs`. Tab completion adds the backslash for you.

try.text: Move into the folder called `shared results`.

command.name: cd -
command.what: Takes you back to the folder you were in before the last cd, and prints its path. Run it again to swap back. Handy when comparing two folders.

try.text: Go into `binder_design/runs/run1`, then use `cd -` to jump back to where you started.

files.~/.bashrc: # settings that run when you log in

quiz.q: `ls` shows a folder named `My Runs`. Which command works?
quiz.why: The name has a capital letter and a space. Quotes keep the two words together as one name, and the case has to match exactly.
